_about: Settings for scripts/review_pack.py ja. Everything in Japanese in this repo is an unreviewed machine draft; Arthur has no Japanese reader, so the order below is what a paid native check should cover first.

choices.what: If time is short, read in this order: (1) Interface sheet, the pink "Must read" rows: paywall and one-time offer first, then sign-in, then onboarding. (2) The Lesson 17_3 sheet, which is the lesson on respect and consent. (3) This sheet. (4) Everything else.
choices.question: Tell us how far you got, so we know what is still unread.

choices.what: The coach speaks in polite です・ます throughout: a calm, direct older brother or trusted 先輩, not a pickup coach and not a therapist. Errors, the paywall and notifications use the same voice.
choices.question: Does it read as a real Japanese man in his thirties would write it? Anything stiff, translated, preachy or cringe?

choices.topic: No 君, no お前, almost no あなた
choices.what: The reader is never called 君 or お前. あなた appears in only two places: the speaker label "You" in scenarios (「あなた」) and one quoted line in lesson 13_4. Everywhere else "you" is dropped, or is 自分 (himself) or こちら (his side of a conversation).
choices.question: Any sentence where it is unclear who is meant? Is こちら natural for the man's side? Should the speaker label be 「あなた」 or 「自分」?

choices.what: This lesson must be at least as strict in Japanese as in English. Examples: 「相手が心地よく感じているとはっきりわかるサインがない限り、決して触れないでください」, 「少しでも身を引いたら、すぐにやめましょう」, 「断られたら、相手に罪悪感を抱かせたり、不機嫌な態度を取ったりせずに受け入れてください」.
choices.question: Is every instruction as firm as the English? Has politeness softened anything into a suggestion?

choices.what: Billing sentences follow the pattern 「本日%1$@が請求されます（最初の1年間分）。その後は月額%2$@で更新されます。App Storeの設定からいつでも解約できます。」. Terms used: サブスクリプション, 利用規約, プライバシーポリシー, 購入を復元, 解約.
choices.where: Interface sheet, area Paywall & one-time offer
choices.question: Are these the words Japanese App Store users expect? Is each sentence unambiguous about what is charged today and what renews? (Wording only; legal questions go to Arthur.)

choices.what: The app joins these from separate strings, so the pieces must read in the fixed order: (a) Home greeting: 「おはようございます」 / 「こんにちは」 / 「こんばんは」 on one line and the user's name on the next; (b) onboarding: bold 「3倍」 followed by 「ありきたりなアドバイス動画を見るより速く上達」; (c) one-time offer: a big "50%" with 「最初の1年間オフ」 under it.
choices.where: Interface sheet: Home, Onboarding, Paywall & one-time offer
choices.question: Do all three read correctly in that order? If not, what order would Japanese need?

choices.what: Onboarding and the paywall quote figures from English-language sources. The numbers are kept as they are and are not presented as findings about Japan.
choices.where: Interface sheet, area Onboarding and Paywall
choices.question: Does any line sound like a claim about Japanese men or women? Any figure that would make a Japanese reader distrust the app?

choices.topic: 声をかける / アプローチ
choices.what: "To approach" is 声をかける. The noun, including one logged approach, is アプローチ (「アプローチを記録」). 声かけ is not used as a noun. ナンパ is avoided everywhere except once, for "pickup lines" in lesson 6_3 (「ナンパの決まり文句」).
choices.question: Natural? Does アプローチ work as a countable thing in the log? Is keeping ナンパ out the right call for this audience?

choices.what: "Opener" is 最初のひと言. Indirect and direct openers are さりげないひと言 and ストレートなひと言; the three types are 好奇心を引くひと言, 推測から入るひと言 and 意見を聞くひと言.
choices.question: Clear and natural, or would a shorter term be better?

choices.what: "Closing" (asking for her contact or the next step) is 次につなげる, never クロージング. An "assumed close" is 前提に立った提案: 「コーヒー、行きましょう。LINE、交換しましょう」.
choices.question: Does 「LINE、交換しましょう」 sound confident and polite, or pushy?

choices.what: "Flirting" is 駆け引き or 恋の駆け引き, and "flirtatious" (of a line) is 恋愛的な含みのある. "Escalate" is 距離を縮める.
choices.where: Lessons and quizzes (courses 17 to 21); course titles on the Interface sheet
choices.question: 駆け引き can also mean tactics or playing games. Does it sound manipulative here? Is there a better everyday word?

choices.what: The three signals are 受け入れのサイン, 礼儀のサイン and 冷たいサイン; "neutral" is どちらともつかない; traffic lights are 青信号, 黄信号, 赤信号. "Calibration" is 相手の反応を見て合わせる.
choices.question: Natural? Is 礼儀のサイン clear as "she is only being polite"?

choices.topic: 空気をリードする / 自分の軸
choices.what: "Frame control" is 空気をリードする; "frame" is 場の空気 when it is the mood he sets and 自分の軸 when it is his own steadiness.
choices.question: Do the two renderings read as one idea? Anything confusing?

choices.what: "Disqualification" (lesson 21_1: not being automatically impressed) is 簡単にはなびかない. Example lines: 「次の一杯をおごってくれるなら」, 「ちょうどいいですね。こちらも、うるさいほうなので」.
choices.question: Does the idea survive? Do the example lines sound playful or rude in Japanese?

choices.what: "Subtext" is 言外のメッセージ, "validating" is 受け止める, "attunement" is 波長を合わせる, "threads" are 糸口 (threading: 糸口をたどる), "observations" and "statements" are 観察 and 自分のひと言, "processed sharing" is 整理のついた話.
choices.question: Any of these that a Japanese reader would not understand at first sight?

choices.what: "Teasing" is からかい, "cheekiness" is いたずら心 (cheeky: いたずらっぽい), "banter" is 軽い掛け合い, "light challenges" are 軽い、遊びの勝負.
choices.question: Natural? Teasing a woman he has just met is riskier in Japanese; do the example lines stay on the safe side?

choices.what: "Volume" and "reps" are 場数; "sticking point" is つまずきポイント; "plateau" is 成長の停滞期; "experimental mindset" is 実験のマインドセット; "outcome independence" is 結果に左右されない.
choices.where: Lessons and quizzes (courses 1 to 5 and 23 to 25)
choices.question: Natural?

choices.what: "Social status" is 社会的な立ち位置, "social proof" is 社会的証明, "home court advantage" is ホームグラウンドの強み, a "regular" is 顔なじみの常連.
choices.question: Does 社会的な立ち位置 read as how the room sees him, not as rank or income?

choices.what: Never translated: Wingman, XP. Kept as katakana loanwords: ミラーリング, グラウンディング, アイコンタクト, ボディランゲージ, マインドセット, エネルギー.
choices.question: Any of these that should be a Japanese word instead? Is エネルギー natural for a person's mood and presence?

choices.what: Every ask for a phone number became an ask for LINE. Instagram is kept in three places where the scene is about her posts or her followers: scenario 15, lesson 21_1 and the quiz question built on that lesson.
choices.question: Right for men of 25 to 55 in Japan? Any line where asking for LINE sounds too fast?

choices.what: Places and habits were swapped where the English would mean nothing: 札幌, 大阪, 福岡 and 熊本 for American cities; a trip to Japan became 台湾; an Uber became a taxi she called; "cereal for dinner" became カップ麺; feet became metres; a barista calls the order, not her name. The advice itself was not changed.
choices.question: Any swap that reads oddly? Any American detail still left that should have been swapped?

choices.what: The women in scenarios keep their foreign names in katakana (ソフィー, ローレン, ナオミ and so on), and he addresses them with さん.
choices.question: Should they have Japanese names instead?

choices.what: 33 lesson paragraphs put a short list or clause in dictionary form inside polite text and then pick it up, as in 「爪を切る。シャワーを浴びる。清潔な服を着る。」 or 「…小さくほほえむ。それだけで、…伝わります」. It mirrors the English fragment lists.
choices.where: Lessons (lesson 1_1 and 6_1 sheets show the style)
choices.question: Acceptable in です・ます writing, or should every sentence end politely?

choices.what: Question stems are polite questions (「…どれですか？」). Options are short dictionary-form or noun phrases; where the stem asks "why", each option ends in 〜から. "All of the above" is 上のすべて and "Both of the above" is 上の両方. Explanations are です・ます.
choices.question: Is that the usual shape of a Japanese quiz? Is 上のすべて right when the app may shuffle the options?

choices.what: Full-width 、。「」！？ in Japanese sentences; half-width digits, % and Latin letters with no space around them (「3倍」, 「50%」, 「Wingmanを」); no space after ！ or ？. A quoted line that ends a sentence is written 「…」。 with the full stop after the bracket.
choices.question: Is 「…」。 acceptable, or should the full stop be dropped? Anything else that looks typeset by a foreigner?

choices.what: A spreadsheet cannot show how lines wrap. Paywall ticks have a hard limit of 18 Japanese characters. One onboarding headline was already shortened because it broke a word across two lines.
choices.question: Any headline or button that is long for a phone screen, or that would break in the middle of a word?

choices.what: Titles are short and mostly in dictionary form or noun phrases: 「空気をリードする」, 「簡単にはなびかない」, 「場数が、慣れをつくる」.
choices.where: Interface sheet, area Courses; lesson sheets
choices.question: Do they read as titles? Any that sounds like a literal translation?

choices.topic: Advice that may not fit Japan
choices.what: The advice was translated as written, not adapted. 63 points where it may land differently in Japan are listed for Arthur under "Cultural flags for Arthur" in docs/localization-ja-progress.md: for example starting conversations on trains, in libraries and at the gym, holding eye contact with strangers, early touch, and treating a quick look-away as no signal.
choices.question: Which of these would a Japanese man be wrong to follow? Which are fine?

rules: Edit only the yellow columns: "Your version", "Status" and "Comment". Leave a row's "Your version" empty if the Japanese is fine, and set Status to OK.
Keep placeholders exactly: %@, %lld, %1$@, %2$lld and so on. They may move within the sentence, but don't change, add or remove them. %% is a percent sign.
Keep link targets: in [利用規約](terms) translate the word in square brackets only; never change (terms) or (privacy).
Paywall ticks have a hard limit (see the "Max length" column). A full-width character counts as two, so a limit of 36 means 18 Japanese characters; longer lines get hidden on small iPhones.
The coach speaks in polite です・ます. Never 君 or お前; あなた only where the sentence fails without it.
Punctuation: full-width 、。「」！？ in Japanese sentences. Digits, % and Latin letters stay half-width with no space around them. No space after ！ or ？.

Adapt rather than translate word for word: if an image or example doesn't land in Japanese, replace it with one that does. Don't change what the advice says; flag advice that doesn't fit Japan in Comment instead.
Don't edit the grey Key column; it is how your changes get back into the app.

example.comment: A button reads better with a verb.
